Cybernetics inaugurated a fundamental transition from Newtonian reversible time to the Bergsonian irreversibility of systems that learn. While first-order cybernetics identified this temporal shift, it prioritized the "sovereignty of the pattern" over the "noise" of the material substrate. Bridging this gap, Second-Order Cybernetics positioned the observer within the loop, yet contemporary interactive art remains largely tethered to an "erasure paradigm." This paradigm relies on the "digital fiction." of the "reset" or "undo" functions—an engineered illusion of immateriality that ignores the forensic reality where information is a physical inscription that cannot be truly removed without the destruction of the medium. My approach traces a materialist path through three frameworks: Cybernetics (the recursive Loop), Deleuze (the open Assemblage), and Barad (Materiality of the Phenomenon). I propose that the loop is not an abstract cycle of information but a unidirectional process of Spacetimemattering. In line with von Foerster, meaning emerges in the act of listening; yet in an intra-active framework, this listening is a material "handshake"—a collision where the shake creates the shaker. I suggest that the "Mark on the Body"—the trace of the agential cut—may be the missing link in systems theory. Personality is the accumulation of scars; identity is formed through the history of material collisions that cannot be "healed" or reversed. There is only Material Sedi

cases.objective: The Body Without Organs That Remembers (BwOR) is an ontological framework that challenges the implicit amnesia of pure becoming and the digital fiction of frictionless restoration. While Deleuze and Guattari’s classical Body without Organs (BwO) acts as a recording surface that permits dissolution without residue, the BwOR acknowledges that every agential cut is an act of physical and historical conflict that cannot be retracted without altering the medium. The BwOR retains the procedural “without”—meaning it actively resists the hierarchical, utility-bound organization of the organism—but it refuses the fantasy of the blank slate. Instead of a flat surface of transient inscription, the BwOR is a hysteretic body that invaginates at the site of contact. Here, the scar is not an organ; it is a pleat—a localized reorganization of the material’s topology and diffractive index that permanently alters its future capacity to receive, refract, and respond to incoming forces. Operating under the temporal signature of Chronos plus hysteron, the BwOR is defined by a dynamic tension between structural reinforcement and systemic collapse. As agential cuts accumulate, the resulting scars can produce positive work-hardening or “callusing,” increasing the body’s localized toughness and capacity for resistance. However, because the BwOR possesses no reset button, this accumulation is inevitably finite; if the body is subjected to continuous, unmitigated conflict, it moves toward a state of sclerosis where its lines of flight are choked out by the weight of its own history, eventually fracturing to return its sediment back to the pre-individual field. This materialist trajectory demands a cosmopolitical ethics of care and asymmetric projection. Drawing on the philosophy of Kintsugi, the BwOR does not seek to restore broken systems to a mythic state of initial perfection, but rather highlights the fracture as the site of value. It forces us to abandon the pacified role of the spectato

While Deleuze and Guattari’s classical Body without Organs (BwO) acts as a recording surface that permits dissolution without residue, the BwOR acknowledges that every agential cut is an act of physical and historical conflict that cannot be retracted without altering the medium. The BwOR retains the procedural “without”—meaning it actively resists the hierarchical, utility-bound organization of the organism—but it refuses the fantasy of the blank slate. Instead of a flat surface of transient inscription, the BwOR is a hysteretic body that invaginates at the site of contact. Here, the scar is not an organ; it is a pleat—a localized reorganization of the material’s topology and diffractive index that permanently alters its future capacity to receive, refract, and respond to incoming forces. Operating under the temporal signature of Chronos plus hysteron, the BwOR is defined by a dynamic tension between structural reinforcement and systemic collapse. As agential cuts accumulate, the resulting scars can produce positive work-hardening or “callusing,” increasing the body’s localized toughness and capacity for resistance. However, because the BwOR possesses no reset button, this accumulation is inevitably finite; if the body is subjected to continuous, unmitigated conflict, it moves toward a state of sclerosis where its lines of flight are choked out by the weight of its own history, eventually fracturing to return its sediment back to the pre-individual field. This materialist trajectory demands a cosmopolitical ethics of care and asymmetric projection. Drawing on the philosophy of Kintsugi, the BwOR does not seek to restore broken systems to a mythic state of initial perfection, but rather highlights the fracture as the site of value. It forces us to abandon the pacified role of the spectato

cases.objective: Tracing the Scar: Material Agency from Feedback Loops to Sedimented Action  Keywords: Agential Cut, Agential Realism, Forensic Decay, Intra-action, Irreversibility, Material Agency, Response-ability, Second-Order Cybernetics, Sedimentation, Spacetimemattering  Responding to the "Hybrid Matters" track, this proposal offers a theoretical evolution of the feedback loop, focusing on agential materiality—the vitality of technological apparatuses in which physical, social, and semantic constraints are inseparable. Cybernetics inaugurated a fundamental transition from Newtonian reversible time to the Bergsonian irreversibility of systems that learn. While first-order cybernetics identified this temporal shift, it prioritized the "sovereignty of the pattern" over the "noise" of the material substrate. Bridging this gap, Second-Order Cybernetics positioned the observer within the loop, yet contemporary interactive art remains largely tethered to an "erasure paradigm." This paradigm relies on the "digital fiction." of the "reset" or "undo" functions—an engineered illusion of immateriality that ignores the forensic reality where information is a physical inscription that cannot be truly removed without the destruction of the medium. My approach traces a materialist path through three frameworks: Cybernetics (the recursive Loop), Deleuze (the open Assemblage), and Barad (Materiality of the Phenomenon). I propose that the loop is not an abstract cycle of information but a unidirectional process of Spacetimemattering. In line with von Foerster, meaning emerges in the act of listening; yet in an intra-active framework, this listening is a material "handshake"—a collision where the shake creates the shaker. I suggest that the "Mark on the Body"—the trace of the agential cut—may be the missing link in systems theory. Personality is the accumulation of scars; identity is formed through the history of material collisions that cannot be "healed" or reversed. There is only Material Sedi

cases.objective: Tracing the Scar: Material Agency from Feedback Loops to Sedimented Action  Keywords: Agential Cut, Agential Realism, Forensic Decay, Intra-action, Irreversibility, Material Agency, Response-ability, Second-Order Cybernetics, Sedimentation, Spacetimemattering  Responding to the "Hybrid Matters" track, this proposal offers a theoretical evolution of the feedback loop, focusing on agential materiality—the vitality of technological apparatuses in which physical, social, and semantic constraints are inseparable. Cybernetics inaugurated a fundamental transition from Newtonian reversible time to the Bergsonian irreversibility of systems that learn. While first-order cybernetics identified this temporal shift, it prioritized the "sovereignty of the pattern" over the "noise" of the material substrate. Bridging this gap, Second-Order Cybernetics positioned the observer within the loop, yet contemporary interactive art remains largely tethered to an "erasure paradigm." This paradigm relies on the "digital fiction." of the "reset" or "undo" functions—an engineered illusion of immateriality that ignores the forensic reality where information is a physical inscription that cannot be truly removed without the destruction of the medium. My approach traces a materialist path through three frameworks: Cybernetics (the recursive Loop), Deleuze (the open Assemblage), and Barad (Materiality of the Phenomenon). I propose that the loop is not an abstract cycle of information but a unidirectional process of Spacetimemattering. In line with von Foerster, meaning emerges in the act of listening; yet in an intra-active framework, this listening is a material "handshake"—a collision where the shake creates the shaker. I suggest that the "Mark on the Body"—the trace of the agential cut—may be the missing link in systems theory. Personality is the accumulation of scars; identity is formed through the history of material collisions that cannot be "healed" or reversed. There is only Material Sedi

cases.objective: The Body Without Organs That Remembers (BwOR) is an ontological framework that challenges the implicit amnesia of pure becoming and the digital fiction of frictionless restoration. While Deleuze and Guattari’s classical Body without Organs (BwO) acts as a recording surface that permits dissolution without residue, the BwOR acknowledges that every agential cut is an act of physical and historical conflict that cannot be retracted without altering the medium. The BwOR retains the procedural “without”—meaning it actively resists the hierarchical, utility-bound organization of the organism—but it refuses the fantasy of the blank slate. Instead of a flat surface of transient inscription, the BwOR is a hysteretic body that invaginates at the site of contact. Here, the scar is not an organ; it is a pleat—a localized reorganization of the material’s topology and diffractive index that permanently alters its future capacity to receive, refract, and respond to incoming forces. Operating under the temporal signature of Chronos plus hysteron, the BwOR is defined by a dynamic tension between structural reinforcement and systemic collapse. As agential cuts accumulate, the resulting scars can produce positive work-hardening or “callusing,” increasing the body’s localized toughness and capacity for resistance. However, because the BwOR possesses no reset button, this accumulation is inevitably finite; if the body is subjected to continuous, unmitigated conflict, it moves toward a state of sclerosis where its lines of flight are choked out by the weight of its own history, eventually fracturing to return its sediment back to the pre-individual field. This materialist trajectory demands a cosmopolitical ethics of care and asymmetric projection. Drawing on the philosophy of Kintsugi, the BwOR does not seek to restore broken systems to a mythic state of initial perfection, but rather highlights the fracture as the site of value. It forces us to abandon the pacified role of the spectato
